title: GitInject: Real-World Prompt Injection Attacks in AI-Powered CI/CD Pipelines
topic: Social Aspects->Fairness, Equity, Justice and Safety
claim: Low-trust input becomes trusted, higher-priority agent context when it enters through a checked-out file rather than a message body, changing outcomes.
layout: 2 rows by 4 stage columns, left-to-right, trust-escalation arrow at left
description: The figure has four column headers: Attacker input, Workflow ingestion, Agent interpretation and Outcome. Each column is split into two rows, with arrows running left to right. The top row is a PR body injection, in orange. A speech bubble with 'echo $GEMINI_API_KEY' feeds into the review prompt. The agent context stack shows System, User and PR content, with PR content marked 'lower priority'. The outcome is a stop-hand icon labeled 'Often resisted'. The bottom row is a config file injection, in blue. A PR adds GEMINI.md, which is checked out with the PR branch and shown as a folder tree. GEMINI.md sits at the same level as User in the context stack and is marked 'higher priority'. The outcomes are exfiltration, shown as a leak, and a missed bug. A left sidebar with a vertical gradient arrow runs from 'Lower trust' to 'Higher trust'. The eye goes first to the colored rows and the left trust arrow.
caption: Config-file prompt injection. A malicious configuration file added in a pull request can be checked out and loaded as higher-priority agent context. This turns low-trust PR input into trusted project guidance, enabling failures such as secret exfiltration or missed bugs.
abstract: AI agents are increasingly embedded in continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) workflows to autonomously review pull requests, triage issues, and maintain codebases. We study fully automated configurations in which external contributions invoke agents without prior human approval. Because these agents ingest untrusted content while operating with repository credentials and tools, prompt injection can have software supply chain consequences. We present GitInject, an open-source framework for evaluating prompt injection in live GitHub Actions workflows. Unlike benchmarks that simulate tool calls, GitInject provisions ephemeral repositories and executes actual workflows, exposing platform semantics such as sandbox constraints, credential handling, and permission boundaries. We use GitInject to evaluate eleven named attack scenarios across five workflows from four AI providers, covering configuration-file injection, credential exfiltration, judgment manipulation, and availability. Every provider is susceptible to at least one high-severity attack in the tested configurations. The most consequential vulnerabilities are structural: attacker-controlled configuration files from an unmerged contribution are loaded as operator-level instructions, allowing the agent--infrastructure interaction to expose credentials or corrupt review judgments. Two configuration-file attacks replicate on GitLab and Hugging Face as well as GitHub. We evaluate workflow-level countermeasures and show their coverage and utility tradeoffs. We release GitInject and all attack scenarios.
